title: Purpose is not a slogan
excerpt: A purpose only means something when it changes a decision. Here’s how to tell whether yours does.
body:
Almost every brand has a purpose statement now. Most of them could be swapped between companies without anyone noticing. That’s the first test worth applying to yours: if a competitor could sign it, it isn’t a purpose yet. It’s a sentiment.

A real purpose costs something. It tells you which customers you’ll turn away, which suppliers you won’t use and which shortcuts you’ll refuse, even when they’d be profitable. If your purpose has never made a decision harder, it hasn’t been tested.

For impact-driven businesses this matters twice over. Customers have learned to be sceptical of good intentions, so the proof has to show up where they can see it: in the sourcing, the packaging, the price and the way the brand speaks.

We start strategy work by asking founders for three decisions the business has made because of what it believes. Those decisions are the purpose. The statement is only the summary.
